pages.text: The morning had promised sunshine. Jujy had heard the promise personally. "Whisker-wiggle roll call!" he announced from the top of the toy shelf. "Today is the Bounce Parade. Everyone will bounce on the trampoline in order of importance, which means me first."
"Ready?" called Azi. "Ready!" called everyone — Dory a beat behind, because she'd been watching a dust mote do something interesting.

The plan was glorious. Azi would bounce highest. Clappy would clap the rhythm. Monkie had written a list of bounce safety rules that nobody had read. Slothie and Baby Slothie would watch from the deck, which was their favorite way to bounce. Azi put on his fastest socks.

But while everyone was lining up by the door, the light changed. It happened quietly, the way gray does. The gold slid off the rug. The window went dim. And then — tap. One small drop knocked on the glass like a little knuckle. Tap. Tap-tap. Then a thousand taps, all at once.
"Rain," said Mama softly from the doorway. "It came instead of the sun." "The trampoline will be wet," said Monkie, checking his list. "Rule four says no wet bouncing."
The Bounce Parade was over before it began.
Something hot and prickly started in Azi's chest, right where the excited feeling had been a minute ago. It pushed up into his throat. And when it came out, it came out squeaky.
"But I waaaant to bounnnnce," said Azi, and his voice bent up at the end like a rusty gate. "I want to go owwwwt."
Mama knelt down so her eyes were next to his eyes. "Hmm," she said gently. "That's your squeaky voice, my love. My ears can't find the words inside a squeak. Can you find your talking voice?"
Azi took a breath. He looked for his words. They were under the squeak — a little crumpled, but there.

"I wanted the Bounce Parade," he said in his talking voice. "And now it's raining. And I don't like it." "There they are," said Mama. "Thank you for your words. That is a true and disappointing thing."
But here is something about feelings: sometimes the words are true, and the feeling is still bigger than the words.
The hot-prickly thing swelled. It filled Azi's chest and his arms and went all the way down into his hands — and his hand grabbed a block from the bin and threw it.
The block flew farther than he meant it to. It bounced off the rug and bumped Dory softly on the ear. Dory blinked. "Hello," she said to the block, rubbing her ear. "Where did you come from?"
Azi froze. The hot feeling was still there, but now a cold one sat down next to it. His hands had done a thing his heart didn't mean.
He went to Dory. He patted the ear where the block had bumped it. "Sorry, Dory." "I forgive you," said Dory. "What were we talking about?"

Mama's voice stayed steady, like a hand on a shoulder. "Azi. Feelings are allowed to be as big as they are. And hands still stay gentle. Even the fullest cloud in the whole sky doesn't throw its rain at anybody." She pointed at the window. "Rain just falls."
They stood at the window together and watched.

"Do you know how rain happens?" Mama asked. "All week long, a cloud drinks. Little sips from puddles. Big sips from the sea. It holds the water, and holds it, and holds it. And when the cloud is so full it cannot hold one single drop more..."
Tap. Tap-tap-tap, said the window. "...it rains. Not because the cloud is bad. Because the cloud is full."
Azi watched the drops race each other down the glass.

"You have clouds too," Mama said. "Right here." She touched his chest, over the hot-prickly place. "They've been drinking all morning. Excited-water. Waiting-water. And then a big gulp of disappointed-water, all at once. No wonder they're full."

Azi's chin wobbled. "You're my whole sky, you know," Mama said. "And even my sky is allowed to rain." "Is it okay?" Azi whispered. "It's more than okay," said Mama. "It's how a heart stays light enough to float."
The first tear came slowly, the way the first raindrop does. Then more.
Azi rained. He rained into Mama's shoulder while she held him, and the sky rained onto the garden, and for a while the inside rain and the outside rain fell together.
Nobody said stop. Nobody said hurry.
Slothie crossed the whole rug — which took a while — and leaned against Azi's leg, warm and heavy. Baby Slothie held on like a small warm comma.
And Clappy, who usually felt things loudly, tapped the softest rhythm on his knee: tap... tap... tap... — a rain song, the quiet kind. Even Clappy knew that some songs are quiet ones.
And then — the way rain always does — it began to slow. Drip. ...Drip.
"Now," Mama whispered, "smell the rain." Azi breathed in through his nose, slow and deep... the green smell of wet garden... one... two... three...
"And blow the clouds away." He blew out, long and soft, and a little circle of fog bloomed on the window glass.
Smell the rain... one... two... three. Blow the clouds... slow... slow... slow.
They did it three times. By the third breath, the hot-prickly thing was gone. And in its place, right in the middle of his chest, there was room.
Outside, the garden was drinking. The kale stood up straighter. The tomatoes shone.
Under a leaf, a honeybee waited politely for the sky to finish.
"Rain has a job," Mama said. "It waters things so they can grow. Tears have a job too. They carry the too-full feeling out... so the light can get back in."
She smiled at the garden. "Some things only grow after rain."
"Do your clouds get full?" Azi asked. "Oh yes," said Mama. "Sometimes when I miss Lita, my clouds fill all the way up."
"So I let it rain a little. And afterward, I can see her face in my heart more clearly."
Azi patted her hand, the way she patted his.
Then Mama took the soft blue blanket and draped it beside the felt thinking-stool by the window.
"This can be your cloud spot," she said. "When your clouds get full, you can come here, where there's room to rain."
"Or squeeze Slothie — he is very squeezable. Or stomp your feet like thunder — thunder is allowed, as long as it doesn't land on anybody."
"Or come find me and say, 'Mama, my clouds are full.' And I will come be your sky-watcher."
"My clouds are full," Azi practiced, in his talking voice. "Perfect," said Mama. "That's the password. It works every time."
By late afternoon, the rain wrung itself out.
The clouds drifted apart, empty and light, and the sun came back to see what it had missed.
The trampoline was still wet. But the driveway was full of puddles — and puddles, Jujy declared, were a kind of parade too.
Azi put on his boots and stomped. Splash!
The very last bit of the big feeling went out through his feet and turned into flying silver water.
Dory splashed the same puddle four times, delighted every time, as if it were brand new.
"The Bounce Parade is postponed until tomorrow," Jujy announced. "By order of me."
Inside, there were warm arepas with honey from Pooh's farm, because after-rain is a hungry time.
And that night, when Azi looked out his bedroom window, the moon was extra bright — washed clean, like it had just had a bath.
The clouds had all gone off to sleep somewhere, empty and light.
And in a twilight-toned room at The Westfield, a boy did the same.

vocab.kidDefinition: so wonderful it makes you want to cheer
a feeling like tiny pins poking you, the way a cactus looks
a thin, high sound like a door that needs oil
shook a tiny bit from side to side, like jelly on a plate
moved to another day, so it can still happen later
warm, round corn cakes you can eat with honey
